title: 'Gagged' immigration judges return to Supreme Court, asserting 'First Amendment black hole'
excerpt: The National Association of Immigration Judges said the Supreme Court’s previous decision in the case has led to a precedential split between court regions that requires settling.
content:
An organization that represents federal immigration judges urged the Supreme Court to intervene in its legal challenge against a Justice Department policy banning them from speaking publicly about their work in their personal capacity. Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty Images

Another chapter in the long-running legal battle over a policy barring the nation’s corps of immigration judges from speaking publicly about their work or immigration more broadly may yet be written, as an employee association and free-speech organization have requested the Supreme Court’s assistance for the second time in the case.

The National Association of Immigration Judges, a non-recognized union representing the around 700 judges at the Justice Department’s Executive Office of Immigration Review, has said the so-called “gag rule” violates its members’ First Amendment rights. The policy, first issued in 2017, made more restrictive in 2020 and revised again in 2021, categorically bars employees’ speech on all matters concerning “agency policies, programs or a subject matter that directly relates to [their] official duties.”

With the help of Columbia University’s Knight First Amendment Institute, NAIJ first sued to end the policy in 2020, but a district court judge dismissed the case in 2023, finding that the group must first pursue its claims administratively, via the Merit Systems Protection Board.

But last year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit revived the complaint, sending the lower court on a fact-finding inquiry as to whether the Trump administration’s effort to take greater control over previously independent agencies like the MSPB had rendered the 1978 Civil Service Reform Act’s intended administrative review scheme meaningless.

The Trump administration appealed that ruling to the Supreme Court, which in turn overturned it on the grounds that the parties in the case had not yet raised such an argument, sending the case back to the Fourth Circuit. In response, the appeals court quietly affirmed the original district court ruling.

But NAIJ wrote in a petition to the Supreme Court that by doing so, the appellate court had created what is known as a circuit split: when legal precedent is in conflict, depending upon where a case is filed. In this instance, the union said the Fourth Circuit’s decision conflicts with a 1996 decision out of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, Weaver v. U.S. Information Agency, a case in which a Voice of America employee challenged a policy requiring agency employees to receive preclearance ahead of any speaking, writing or teaching engagement.

“After being admonished for violating this requirement, [Weaver] filed an amended complaint challenging that sanction in addition to the policy,” NAIJ wrote. “The court dismissed Weaver’s challenge to the admonishment, reasoning that it was remediable under the CSRA as a ‘prohibited personnel practice.’ But the court treated her challenge to the policy differently, holding that the district court had jurisdiction over ‘a simple pre-enforcement attack on a regulation restricting employee speech.’”

The union argued that its case is similar, and that because EOIR’s gag order chills constitutionally protected activity, it creates the type of “here-and-now” injury that cannot be remediated after months or years of exhausting plaintiffs’ administrative avenues for redress.

“Review of the Fourth Circuit’s decision is warranted now because it threatens to create a First Amendment black hole,” NAIJ wrote. “Under the Fourth Circuit’s application of Thunder Basin, administrations of both political parties could enact sweeping prior restraints on the speech of federal employees without any guarantee of judicial review.”

In a statement Tuesday, NAIJ President Holly D’Andrea said the gag rule not only hurts her organization’s members, but also impedes the American public’s broader understanding of immigration issues.

“Judges do not turn in their right to free speech when they put on the robe,” she said. “Our country was designed to be governed by public reason, not private silence. Silencing judges deprives the public of a key perspective on the rule of law.”
